拱頂吉他常歸功奧維爾·吉布森，其1898年曼陀林專利亦適用於吉他，採用提琴式拱面: The archtop guitar is often credited to Orville Gibson, whose 1898 mandolin patent also applied to guitars and used a violin-style arched top and back; earlier patents exist, Merrill in 1896 and Back in 1893. In 1922 Lloyd Loar redesigned new models for Gibson, which became the model for the jazz guitar. In 1936 the first commercially successful Spanish-style electric guitar took the guitar into jazz orchestras; in 1951 a single-cutaway two-pickup model combined acoustic and electric; in 1955 a thin body reduced feedback. It was later made by American and European firms, declined in the 1970s and 80s, and revived in the 1990s through boutique makers and mass production.

In early jazz bands it stood out in the ensemble because of its volume; later it appeared in country music, early rock and roll and mainstream pop and rock, and was taken up by electric blues players. Both purely acoustic and semi-acoustic versions can accompany or play solo.

Its features are six strings, an arched top and back, an adjustable bridge, violin-style f-holes and a tailpiece behind the bridge, a fixed bridge or a tremolo tailpiece; the neck usually joins at the fourteenth fret. Its timbre is common in jazz, blues and rockabilly, and it is used in big bands, swing and country music.
